headline: July 13, and Washington's Already Fishing Like Mid-August
subhead: The eastern wall lit up early again this year, and if you know why Washington runs ahead of the pack, you already know where to point the bow.
body_markdown:
Thirteen days into July and Washington Canyon is fishing like it's the second week of August. That's not hype, that's just the calendar catching up to what the water already told us back in mid-June. I've run this canyon long enough to know the pattern: Washington sits far enough south and far enough west that the Gulf Stream's warm filaments find the eastern wall before they ever reach Wilmington or Baltimore to the north. Every year, without fail, we're pulling yellowfin out of this canyon two to three weeks before boats running out of Cape May or Manasquan start talking about it. This year's no different, maybe a hair earlier.

What's happening right now is a warm push riding up onto the eastern wall, roughly the 38°18' to 38°22' line, 73°00' to 73°08', where the shelf breaks from the 100-fathom curve down into the canyon proper. That's the color change we've been working — clean blue water butting up against the greener inshore stuff, and that seam has been holding bait and holding fish. Boats working the temp break with the spread down have been picking off yellowfin in the 40 to 65-pound class, mixed in with a scattering of smaller schoolies that come through in wolf packs on the troll. Small Green Machines, naked ballyhoo behind a chin-weighted Sea Witch, and a couple of Ilanders in dark colors have been the difference-makers. Nothing fancy — just get the spread tight to the seam and let the current do the rest.

The deep-drop bite at night has been the more consistent producer if I'm being honest with you. Bigeye have been sitting on the wall in 350 to 450 fathoms, and the guys willing to put in the dark hours with squid strips and glow sticks on the deep-drop rigs are getting rewarded. It's not a numbers game — one or two quality bites a night, fish in the 100 to 180-pound range — but for mid-July that's ahead of where we usually are. I had a report from a boat working the western edge of the canyon head last week that put two bigeye in the box before 3 a.m. and never had another sniff after sunrise. That's the nature of that fishery right now — short windows, quality fish, and you need to be exactly where the current is stacking bait against the wall.

White marlin have shown up on the pinnacle just inshore of the canyon proper, working that 40 to 50-fathom structure where the bottom breaks up sharp. Dink ballyhoo behind small skirts, a dredge down the middle, and light drags — that's the recipe. It's not a red-hot bite, I want to be straight with you, more of a two-to-four fish morning if you find the right piece of structure and the current is moving right. But for this early in the season, marlin showing on the pinnacle already tells me the biomass pushing up the shelf is ahead of a normal year.

Mahi have been scattered rather than stacked — a few here, a few there, mostly holding under floating debris and weed lines on the run out past the 60-fathom line. Nothing like the August pattern where you find a real mat of sargassum and load the box. Right now it's more a matter of running lines and eyes open, pitching small chuggers or a bit of ballyhoo when you spot color or debris. Decent fish, 8 to 15 pounds, but you're working for every one of them.

Wahoo have made an early appearance too, which fits the theme of this whole season. High-speed trolling along the eastern wall at first light, planers running Braid Marauders and small Ilanders at 12 to 14 knots, has produced a few scattered fish in the 40 to 60-pound range. It's not the August wahoo pattern where you can count on multiple fish a trip — this is more opportunistic, a bonus if you're already working the wall for tuna at dawn. But again, seeing wahoo this early tells me the water column out there is set up warm and stable, not just a surface skim of Gulf Stream water that'll blow out with the next cold front.

Honest read on the week: this isn't a slam-dunk bite. You need to find the seam, work the color change, and be willing to put in the overnight hours for the bigeye. The guys running blind troll patterns without checking the temp break have had quiet days. The guys who worked the eastern wall where the warm filament is pinching against the canyon edge have had good ones. That's Washington in July — it rewards the boats that read the water instead of just running numbers on a chartplotter.

Looking ahead, if this warm filament holds its position on the eastern wall through the weekend — and there's no strong reason yet to think it's sliding — I'd keep working that 38°18' to 73°05' box for the yellowfin and push the deep drop rigs out toward the 400-fathom curve after dark for bigeye. If the eddy slides east like it sometimes does after a blow, I'd shift attention to the pinnacle for marlin and work the shallower structure instead of chasing open water. Either way, Washington's running ahead of pace again this year, and I don't expect that gap to close anytime soon.
